title: Investor Psychology
blurb: Why clients buy high and sell low — and how to spot the bias, answer it, and keep the plan on track.

rows: New employees (all sections), sales team (talk-tracks, role-plays, niche topics); investors as awareness material
About 81 minutes of lessons, plus role-play and the final quiz
Each L.E.A.R.N. stage has: what to know, how to do it, a talk-track, and the investor takeaway

sources: SEBI Master Circular for Mutual Funds (current edition)

lessons.title: The behaviour gap: why clients earn less than their funds
How the gap opens: three costly moves
Guardrails (2): emergency fund, STP, cooling-off, pre-commitment
Review rhythm: calendar, less checking, rebalance by rule
Bias library (1): loss aversion, herd, recency, anchoring
Bias library (2): disposition, overconfidence, confirmation, mental accounting
Bias library (4): six more niche biases
Compliance: dos, don'ts and the final check

a: The difference between the return a fund delivers and the return its investors actually earn, caused by buying after rallies and selling after falls.
Fast: instant, emotional, driven by fear and greed. Slow: deliberate, checks the plan. Under stress, the fast system usually wins.

cards.q: How much more do losses hurt?
a: Roughly twice as much as equal gains feel good (Kahneman & Tversky, Prospect Theory).
Euphoria. Most investors buy here, just when risk is highest.
Despondency. Most investors sell here, often just before the recovery.
Nifty 50 fell about 40% in a month; closed at 7,610 on 23 March 2020; rose about 99% from that low by 8 February 2021.
A written plan, agreed in calm times, of what the client will and won't do if markets fall 20%.
No switch or redemption is decided on the same day as a big market move.
Rebalance when the allocation drifts beyond an agreed band (e.g. ±5%). It forces trimming what rose and adding to what fell.
"Would I suggest this if it hadn't done well last year?"
Show progress to goals in rupees and %, and 3–5 year XIRR vs benchmark, not a list of red and green funds.
Call clients before they call you, starting with recent and first-time investors.
Losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains please.
Sounds like: "The market fell, let me stop my SIP."
Say: Your SIP is buying more units cheaper now.
Following what everyone else is doing.
Sounds like: "Everyone is buying small-caps."
Say: Let's check it fits your allocation first.
Over-weighting the latest results.
Sounds like: "This fund gave 40% last year."
Say: Let's look at its 5-year record and bad years.
Fixating on a reference number like the buy price.
Sounds like: "I'll sell once it's back to my cost."
Say: Your buying price doesn't affect what the fund does next.
Selling winners too early, holding losers too long.
Sounds like: "Sell the winner, keep the loser."
Say: Let's judge each fund on merit.
Over-rating one's ability to pick or time.
Sounds like: "I'll time the market myself."
Say: Even professionals struggle to time markets.
Seeking only information that agrees.
Sounds like: "Everything I read says it will go up."
Say: Let's look at the case against it too.
Treating money differently by its source.
Sounds like: "This bonus is free money to take a risk with."
Say: It's still your money; put it toward a goal.
Staying in a bad choice because of what's already put in.
Sounds like: "I've held this 5 years, I can't exit now."
Say: Is it the best fund for the next five years?
Doing nothing because change feels hard.
Sounds like: "My money is fine in savings for now."
Say: Doing nothing is also a decision; inflation charges for it.
Avoiding action for fear of regretting it.
Sounds like: "What if I invest and it falls tomorrow?"
Say: Let's stagger it through an STP.
Preferring what is known, e.g. employer shares.
Sounds like: "Most of my money is in my company's shares."
Say: Your salary already depends on that company.
"I knew it all along", after the fact.
Sounds like: "It was obvious the market would crash."
Say: It always looks obvious afterwards; we plan, not predict.
Checking too often makes normal swings feel like losses.
Sounds like: "I check daily and it stresses me."
Say: Let's look quarterly; daily moves are noise.
Trusting someone because they sound expert.
Sounds like: "A big YouTuber recommended this."
Say: Let's check they're SEBI-registered and it fits your plan.
Same fact, different reaction depending on wording.
Sounds like: "90% chance of gain" vs "10% chance of loss"
Say: Present risk both ways, and in rupees.
Expecting a reversal because of a streak.
Sounds like: "It's risen 5 months straight, it must fall now."
Say: Markets have no memory; stick to your allocation.
Valuing what you own more than you'd pay for it.
Sounds like: "I inherited these shares, I can't sell them."
Say: Would you buy them today with fresh money?
Preferring spending now over saving for later.
Sounds like: "I'll start investing after the new car."
Say: A small SIP now buys years of compounding.
Favouring last year's winners or easy-to-sell products.
Sounds like: "This fund is hot, every client should get it."
Say: Use the suitability checklist every time.

questions.q: What is the behaviour gap?
o: The gap between NAV and market price
The difference between a fund's return and the return its investors actually earn
The difference between direct and regular plan returns
The gap between a benchmark and its category average
questions.why: The difference between a fund's return and the return its investors actually earn. It opens up when investors buy after rallies and sell after falls.

questions.q: According to Kahneman and Tversky, losses feel roughly how painful compared with equal gains?
questions.why: About twice. Losses loom roughly twice as large as gains (Prospect Theory).

questions.q: "I'll sell once it's back to what I paid." Which bias?
questions.why: Anchoring. The client is fixated on the purchase price as a reference point.

questions.q: "This fund gave 40% last year, let's buy it." Which bias?
questions.why: Recency. Over-weighting the most recent results.

questions.q: "Everyone in my WhatsApp group is buying this small-cap fund." Which bias?
questions.why: Herd / FOMO. Following the crowd, often after a rally.

questions.q: "I check my portfolio every day and it stresses me." Which bias?
questions.why: Myopic loss aversion. Frequent checking makes normal swings feel like losses.

questions.q: "I've held this fund for 5 years, I can't exit now." Which bias?
questions.why: Sunk cost. Past investment is spent; the question is the next five years.

questions.q: "My money is fine in savings for now." Which bias?
questions.why: Status quo / inertia. Doing nothing feels safe but has a cost.

questions.q: At which point in the emotion cycle do most investors buy?
questions.why: Euphoria. They buy near the peak, when risk is highest.

questions.q: Which guardrail best counters regret aversion when investing a large lump sum?
questions.why: An STP over 6–12 months. Staggering entry means no single day decides the outcome.

questions.q: What does the cooling-off rule say?
o: No switch or redemption on the same day as a big market move
questions.why: No switch or redemption on the same day as a big market move. It stops panic or FOMO decisions in the heat of the moment.

questions.q: What is the best way to frame an annual review?
o: Show progress to each goal in rupees and %
Lead with the latest market headline
Show the best and worst fund only
questions.why: Show progress to each goal in rupees and %. Goals and long periods counter short-term framing and recency.

questions.q: What is the first step of the crisis playbook?
o: Call clients before they call you, newest investors first
questions.why: Call clients before they call you, newest investors first. Proactive calls prevent panic decisions.

questions.q: What was the Nifty 50's closing low on 23 March 2020?
questions.why: 7,610. It then rose about 99% from that low by 8 February 2021.

questions.q: Which statement to a client is compliant?
o: "In 2020 markets recovered, but past recoveries don't guarantee future ones."
"I promise your SIP will be positive by March."
"Stay invested; losses are impossible over 3 years."
questions.why: "In 2020 markets recovered, but past recoveries don't guarantee future ones.". Use history as context, never as a promise.

questions.q: Is knowing about biases enough to stop them affecting decisions?
o: No — knowing doesn't switch them off; systems and habits do
questions.why: Knowing doesn't switch them off; systems and habits do.

questions.q: Can distributors be affected by recency bias?
o: Yes — e.g. pitching last year's top fund to every client
questions.why: e.g. pitching last year's top fund to every client.

questions.q: A client redeems during a fall. What should you check first?
o: Whether it reflects a genuine need: job loss, medical expense, or a goal that is due
questions.why: First check for a genuine need: job loss, medical expense, or a goal that is due.

questions.q: Rebalancing by rule usually means:
o: Trimming some of what has risen and adding to what fell
questions.why: It forces “sell high, buy low”, the opposite of instinct.

questions.q: Is it acceptable to tell a client markets will recover within 12 months?
o: No — never promise a recovery or its timing
questions.why: Never promise a recovery or its timing.

questions.q: Markets have fallen 15% in a month. A client with a 10-year goal calls to stop all SIPs. How do you respond?
o: Agree and stop all SIPs immediately

Acknowledge the feeling; reconnect to the goal and 10-year horizon; explain the SIP buys more units at lower prices; remind them of their signed plan; use history as context without promising recovery; record the call
Promise the market will recover next month
Switch everything to debt at once
questions.why: Acknowledge the feeling; reconnect to the goal and 10-year horizon; explain that the SIP is buying more units at lower prices; remind them of their signed plan; use history as context without promising recovery; record the call.

questions.q: A client wants to move everything into a small-cap fund “everyone in the WhatsApp group” is buying. How do you respond?
o: Name it gently as following the crowd; check fit with the target allocation and risk profile; explain popular often means it has already run up; if appropriate, limit it to a planned slice; never pitch using FOMO
questions.why: Name it gently as following the crowd; check fit with the target allocation and risk profile; explain that popular often means it has already run up; if appropriate, limit it to a planned slice; never pitch using FOMO.

questions.q: A client has ₹20 lakh in a savings account “until the market settles”. What do you suggest?
o: Show the cost of waiting (inflation, missed compounding); link the money to specific goals; propose an STP from a liquid or debt fund into equity over 6–12 months to reduce regret
Wait for a crash before investing anything
Put it all in a sectoral fund now
questions.why: Show the cost of waiting (inflation, missed compounding); link the money to specific goals; propose an STP from a liquid or debt fund into equity over 6–12 months to reduce regret.

questions.q: An IT employee has 70% of their wealth in their employer's shares. What is the bias, and what do you do?
o: No bias — employer shares are safe
Familiarity bias. Explain the double risk to job and savings together; propose gradual diversification over time, with tax implications discussed with their CA
Sell everything in one day regardless of tax
questions.why: Familiarity bias. Explain the double risk to job and savings together; propose gradual diversification over time, with tax implications discussed with their CA.

questions.q: Your manager asks you to pitch last year's top fund to every client this month. What do you do?
o: Pitch it to everyone as instructed
Recognise the distributor's own recency bias; raise suitability concerns; use the checklist and recommend the fund only where it fits a client's goals and risk profile; ask the guard question
questions.why: Recognise the distributor's own recency bias; raise suitability concerns; use the checklist and recommend the fund only where it fits a client's goals and risk profile; ask the guard question.
